summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The lower house of Parliament voted 43-1 in June 2019 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, which had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are reported as suspended for lack of standardised guidelines, while other documentation describes a procedure requiring a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation before a marker change is permitted. Either way, a visitor whose documents do not match their presentation should expect the marker on the card to govern how authorities treat them.

That gap has direct consequences. Trans people are recorded as more than four times as likely to experience assault. In a November 2024 broadcast report, a 49-year-old trans woman described having nowhere to report violence: police dismissed her cases because her identity card reads male, treating the matter as one where 'both parties are men', families pressure victims to accept abuse as fate, and assistance routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee moves slowly. Anti-trans violence therefore attracts practical impunity despite formal decriminalisation.

Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 parliamentary session but deferred pending that year's election; whether it has been revived is not established in the sources.

Some protective machinery exists at official level. The Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation. A 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires health-care providers to deliver care sensitive to sexual orientation and gender identity, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse orientations and identities. The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians, alongside consultation workshops with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.
tangentialFactors:
Public trans visibility in Bhutan remains exceptional rather than ordinary. A national broadcaster's feature profiled Dechen, described as one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, started around 2013-2014, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population.

Reporting from 2015 described very little persecution or violence alongside near-total social invisibility, with no shared language for gay or trans identities and lesbianism under-recognised. That account predates decriminalisation and the 2024 assault data, which point to a different picture for trans people specifically.

The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues, yet Rainbow Bhutan's director states that most LGBTQ youths drop out of school; of 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below age 19.
localsOnly:
LGBTIQ organisations may register in Bhutan, though activists describe the process as lengthy and burdensome.

Changing the gender marker on legal identification documents requires submitting a medical note together with a supporting letter from a civil society organisation, according to one documentation of the process; another source reports that administrative marker changes are suspended pending standardised guidelines.

Residents report that families pressure victims of violence to accept it as fate, and that help routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee is slow to arrive.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of gender-marker changes is unresolved in the sources: one inventory entry states that administrative changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines, another describes an active procedure requiring a medical note and a civil society letter. Both are recorded above; a visitor should confirm current practice with the relevant Bhutanese authority before relying on either.

No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules for trans visitors, including whether gender markers on passports are checked or questioned on arrival. This is not sourced either way.

The inventory does not establish whether Bhutan has hate-crime or hate-speech provisions covering gender identity, nor whether the 2018 gender-neutral marriage bill has been reintroduced since the election that deferred it. Both remain unresolved.
